label: GPT-6.1 Terra
output:
**An open letter about the pier and buoy temperatures**

Hi everyone,

A few people have asked why my pier logger reads warmer than the offshore buoy. One reader sent me an overlay of the two records, which was genuinely helpful: it showed that the gap tracks sunny afternoons.

The short answer is that the two instruments are measuring different patches of water. In October, the pier logger averaged **15.9°C**, while the buoy averaged **14.1°C**—a gap of about **1.8°C**. In winter, that gap shrinks to around **0.4°C**.

The logger is strapped to a piling three metres down and about 150 metres from shore. The buoy is roughly 25 kilometres offshore, with its sensor just below the surface in deep water. Shallow nearshore water can warm in the sun, especially on bright afternoons. The bay is also sheltered from some of the upwelling that keeps offshore water cold. So a warmer pier reading is not, by itself, evidence that the logger is faulty.

That said, I do check it. I run a two-point check in an ice bath and a room-temperature bath, comparing the logger with a lab reference thermometer. At the last check, in September 2026, the logger’s offset was **+0.12°C**, well inside its specification and far smaller than the October gap.

The logger records every 10 minutes. I pull it and download the data every six weeks, and replace the battery once a year. In August, it came up with a barnacle colony and a decorator crab living on the housing. I scraped it clean; the readings didn’t change.

Neither record is “the right one” for every purpose. The buoy tells us about offshore surface water; the pier logger tells us what’s happening near the pier at three metres. If you’re diving the breakwater, the pier reading is likely to be more relevant.

If you’d like the raw CSV, please email me and I’ll be happy to share it.
